title: 13 Ideas to Help Boost Homework Completion Rates
author: Craig Barton
summary: Barton opens with the problem that many schools see low homework completion, citing a school with 15 percent completion for online maths homework in Year 9, and offers thirteen practical ideas to raise it. Several rest on research: shorter and more frequent tasks build habit, quality and interest predict effort, and an easy first question reduces drop-out. Others are matters of school culture and routine, such as establishing the norm that everyone completes homework through the profusion and prominence of the behaviour, removing barriers, standardising format, fixing hand-out and collection days, and applying consistent sanctions. He insists that online homework be treated as seriously as written work and that students know what to do when stuck. The most important idea, saved for last, is making homework feed into lessons so it is seen as part of one machine rather than a separate chore. The piece closes with a plug for Eedi but the argument stands independently.
points: Students will put in more effort if they understand why a homework is set, so the teacher should name its purpose and check that students can say it back.
Online homework must not become set-and-forget; following up on non-completion and good work as with paper homework signals that it matters.
Habit drives completion: shorter, more frequent homeworks, a standard format, and fixed hand-out and hand-in days make the routine automatic.
Norms are built by increasing the profusion and prominence of the desired behaviour, illustrated by Beth Kearns using parent contact, public celebration and school social media.
Homework that feeds visibly into lessons, for example by reteaching the worst-answered questions or using it for the Do Now, gains student buy-in.
quotes: The sad truth is that lots of students simply do not engage with homework at all, or put in whatever effort is just high enough to avoid the wrath of the teacher. And the old cliche rings true: often it is the very students who need to engage with homework the most that simply do not.
But students pick up on this “set and forget” approach, and low completion rates for online homework especially are sure to follow.
A key reason for this is habit. The more homework students complete, the more completing homework becomes a part of their routine.
Norms in school are so powerful. Few students want to be different from the crowd. So, to boost homework completion rates we need to establish the norm that everyone completes their homework.
Make the first question of every homework the easiest one - possibly even too easy compared to the rest of the homework - in order to give students the boost they may need to get started and persist.
Consistency is the key here. As soon as students see you are not always following through, it is another reason for them not to complete their homework.

If however, classwork and homework are regarded as two key components of the same machine that feed into and mutually reinforce each other, then you stand a much better chance of students buying into homework.
